title: Good-Better-Best Estimate Engine for Vet Clinics
one_liner: AI scribes are turning into a free feature, so the money moves to the moment a client sees the estimate: automate tiered spectrum-of-care plans that turn declines into partial acceptance.
customer: Emergency/urgent-care hospitals and 2-10 DVM independent general practices, where estimates over $1,000 are routine. Buyer is the practice owner or hospital manager.
problem: Per the briefing, 85% of vet professionals say clients decline care at estimates of $1,000 or less, and 86% alter treatment plans weekly for financial reasons. Estimates are still hand-built as one gold-standard plan, so declines are lost revenue and a source of moral distress (33% of vets find below-gold care distressing). Nobody logs why clients decline.
solution: Reads the diagnosis or SOAP note from any scribe or PIMS and drafts three clinician-approved tiers: full workup, stabilize-and-monitor, and essential/palliative. Each tier is priced from the clinic's own fee schedule, with consent language, expected-outcome ranges and stage-gated steps (approve step 1 now, decide step 2 after results). Financing and insurance pre-check sit on the same screen. Every decline reason is captured and feeds a protocol library written with boarded clinicians. Ships as a browser overlay on the PIMS estimate screen.
why_now: IDEXX bought the CoVet AI scribe on 2026-09-16 and says it will stay compatible with non-IDEXX systems. That marks documentation AI as a bundled strategic feature and squeezes standalone scribes. Clinic visits have reportedly fallen three years running, and price, not demand, is the constraint.
revenue_model: SaaS at $300-600 per clinic per month, plus an optional success fee of 3-5% of incremental accepted revenue measured against a pre-pilot baseline. Later, anonymized decline-reason data sold to insurers and lenders.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders think the AI prize is saving doctors' time on notes. The budget line is revenue at the decision moment, and the scribe is just a commodity input to it. The decline reason is a dataset nobody collects, and it is what financiers and insurers most want.
first_30_days: Sign 5 ER/urgent-care sites and 5 independents. Take each site's last 20 de-identified declined estimates, have a contract boarded vet rebuild them as three-tier plans, and run a 4-week pilot tracking acceptance rate. Charge a $1,500 pilot fee. Prototype the browser overlay with an LLM plus the clinic's fee-schedule export.

title: Seller-Financing Rails for Paid-Off Homeowners
one_liner: A compliant seller-carry-in-a-box that lets free-and-clear homeowners become the bank, with underwriting, servicing, tax packaging and a note-sale exit.
customer: Retiring owners with paid-off homes and large embedded gains (SF, Chicago and other coastal markets), their listing agents and attorneys, and buyers who cannot or will not take a 7.5% bank loan (self-employed, thin-file, relocating).
problem: 30-year rates are about 7.4-7.6%, 58% more sellers than buyers and 42.5% of listings have price cuts, so deals die on financing. About 40% of owner-occupied homes carry no mortgage, and their owners could earn a better yield than deposits while deferring capital-gains tax through an installment sale. Today seller-carry is a handshake plus a lawyer, with no underwriting, servicing or exit, and federal and state rules on ability-to-repay and balloons make DIY risky.
solution: A packaged workflow: buyer ability-to-repay underwriting, state-specific note and deed-of-trust documents, a licensed sub-servicer with tax and insurance escrow, installment-sale tax packets, and a standing bid to buy the note when the seller wants liquidity. Agents get a listing-side toggle, 'seller-carry available', that widens the buyer pool.
why_now: Record buyer's market with rising rates makes sellers' cheapest concession their own balance sheet. Futures now price a 5% Fed funds rate by end-2027, which makes note yields attractive, and AI document and underwriting tooling makes small-loan servicing economical.
revenue_model: 1-1.5% origination fee paid by the buyer, $25-35 per month servicing, a 1-2 point spread on note sales, and an agent subscription tier.
non_obvious_insight: The best 'rate buydown' is not paying points to a bank but becoming the bank. Free-and-clear boomers hold the largest un-deployed lending balance sheet in housing and are one compliance product away from using it. Sellers with gains above the primary-residence exclusion also get a tax reason to spread proceeds over years.
first_30_days: Choose one state with a workable seller-finance framework and partner with a licensed originator and servicer there. Recruit 30 listing agents from local groups. Sell a $499 flat seller-carry consult to 10 sellers and track how many close. Have counsel sign off on the federal seller-financing exemption conditions before any live deal.

title: Verified Cool-Night Rooms for Heat-Stressed Europe
one_liner: Cheap in-room sensors prove a hotel room stays below about 26C at night, sold as a certificate, a refund guarantee and a machine-readable rating for booking agents.
customer: Hotels, B&Bs and STR operators in Greece, Italy, Spain, Croatia, Portugal and Turkey, with OTAs, agent builders and insurers as secondary buyers.
problem: Summer heat makes 'air-conditioned' meaningless, since old units, weak cooling and poor insulation leave rooms hot at night. Nobody measures indoor night temperature, so complaints turn into refund disputes. Rerouted demand into Turkey and Southern Europe, and a focus on 'value for money', make heat a rising complaint.
solution: Fit a USD 10-15 wireless sensor per room in about 10 minutes. It logs a nightly indoor temperature curve, and we issue a 'Cool Night verified' certificate showing the share of nights below the threshold, with a public verification page and JSON feed for AI agents and metasearch. Hotels also get a dashboard to find and fix problem rooms, and can add a hotel-funded heat refund guarantee.
why_now: Repeated European heatwaves, cheap connected sensors, and AI booking assistants that need structured, verifiable attributes because star ratings and 'AC yes/no' are uninformative. Booking's commoditisation of listings makes measured differentiation valuable to independents.
revenue_model: EUR 6-9 per room per month, a EUR 150 install kit, an annual certification fee, and data licensing to platforms.
non_obvious_insight: Comfort is the one hotel attribute that is physically measurable yet almost never measured. In a world of agent-driven booking, a verified physical attribute becomes a ranking signal.
first_30_days: Recruit 30 hotels in Athens, Crete, Sicily and Puglia using off-the-shelf sensors. Offer a free 30-day 'truth test' and publish an anonymised heat report for press. Convert 10 to paid subscriptions.

title: Flight Recorder for AI-Drafted Police Reports
one_liner: Vendor-agnostic middleware that captures the AI draft, every officer edit and timestamp, then issues a court-ready authorship record, the process-based 'human-made' proof creators lack, so prosecutors will accept AI-assisted reports.
customer: Police departments and sheriffs' offices ($60-150 per officer per year), city and county attorneys and DA offices that must vouch for reports, and public defender offices (per-case discovery audits).
problem: Tools such as Axon's Draft One write narratives from body-cam audio, and reporting in 2025 said original AI drafts are not retained (prior knowledge). California SB 524 (effective 2026) requires disclosure of AI use and retention of first drafts, Utah requires disclaimers, and King County prosecutors said in 2024 they would reject AI-assisted reports (prior knowledge). Defense has the same failure mode: a SOCOM analyst's chatbot fabricated a ship's cargo manifest that was formatted as an official intelligence summary, with no provenance layer in the workflow.
solution: A capture layer inside the report editor or records-management system logs the body-cam transcript hash, the AI draft, each officer edit as a diff, and time-on-task, with per-paragraph officer attestations ('I observed' or 'I reviewed'). It emits a signed content-credential-style record attached to the report, a redacted discovery packet for defense, and a DA-portal view that applies each office's acceptance rules.
why_now: State laws requiring disclosure and draft retention are in force in 2026. AI report-writing is spreading while DA acceptance remains the gate. Process-based provenance standards (C2PA) now exist, and GenAI.mil's 2M-user rollout shows the same official-looking-AI-text problem is arriving federally.
revenue_model: Per-officer SaaS, per-case discovery-packet fees to public defenders, and later federal licenses for labeling AI-assisted analytic products.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck to AI report-writing is admissibility and credibility, not accuracy, and the real gatekeepers are DAs, not police chiefs. A DA who publishes an acceptance standard requiring a verifiable authorship record forces every vendor to comply, so give the standard to DAs first and sell the ledger to departments second.
first_30_days: Get one DA's office in a state with an SB 524-style law to co-draft an acceptance standard. Prototype a Word and Google Docs add-in plus a records-system-neutral upload, pilot it with 2 small departments already testing AI report tools, and offer public defenders an 'AI-report discovery audit' service.

title: Mitigation Grant Packets for Small Towns
one_liner: A packet factory and compliance tracker that gets small governments through FEMA and state mitigation grants without clawbacks.
customer: Municipalities under 25,000 people, counties, tribal governments, special districts and state emergency-management agencies, paid from management-cost lines.
problem: BRIC was cancelled in April 2025, restored by court order, reinstated Mar 18 2026 with $1B, and applications closed July 23 2026. Small governments lack staff for benefit-cost analysis, environmental and historic review, procurement and match documentation, and then risk clawbacks. California's new Safe Homes Grant and SB 894 revolving loan need local administration.
solution: Standardized templates for the top project types (culvert upsizing, generators, elevation, defensible space, floodproofing, safe rooms), covering benefit-cost analysis, environmental checklists and procurement. Add post-award compliance and drawdown tracking, built for several programs since BRIC timing is uncertain.
why_now: Federal funding restarted but is unstable. States are building their own programs, and big consultants ignore small jobs.
revenue_model: $6-20K fixed fee per packet and $1-2K/month compliance retainers.
non_obvious_insight: Government grants are gated by paperwork, and the volume of unserved demand sits in towns that big consultants skip.
first_30_days: Cold-email 200 town managers in high-hazard states with a free readiness scan, and sign 3 pilots.

title: Data Centers That Make Water From Waste Heat
one_liner: Containerized membrane-distillation skids that use a liquid-cooled data center's own warm return loop to turn cooling-tower blowdown or brackish well water into clean make-up water.
customer: Colo and AI-hosting operators in Texas, Arizona and Nevada facing water audits, plus immersion-cooled bitcoin and HPC hosts whose loops run hot. Operators buy or lease; fabs later.
problem: Data centers are the target of water regulation (Texas freeze and reporting crime, Australian standards, New York and Ohio actions), and cooling blowdown creates a discharge headache. Desalination was uneconomic because heat was expensive, but a data center produces heat it must remove anyway.
solution: Integrate membrane-distillation modules from an existing OEM with the site's warm loop (liquid-cooled racks now return water at roughly 45-65 C, my estimate). The skid concentrates blowdown and produces distillate for make-up water, cutting purchased water and discharge volume. Add a metering-and-ledger layer that produces a verified 'water-negative' claim. First product: a 10-50 m3/day skid.
why_now: A 2025 Chinese plant reported desal near $0.28/m3 using waste heat (not fully verified). Liquid cooling is spreading, and regulators and lenders now ask for verified water use.
revenue_model: $250-600k equipment sale per skid, or water-as-a-service at roughly $1.5-3/m3 plus O&M. Regulatory value (fewer permits, less discharge) is the closing argument.
non_obvious_insight: Membrane distillation lost to reverse osmosis because it needs large amounts of heat, and a data center offers abundant heat that must be removed, so its energy cost is effectively negative. The villain of the water story becomes the equipment that solves it.
first_30_days: Find three immersion-cooled mining or HPC hosts in Texas with 55-65 C loops. Partner with an MD module OEM for a 5 m3/day trial unit ($60-120k). Sign an LOI with a host for a 90-day pilot that shares data on kWh-thermal per m3, TDS and fouling.

title: DNA-Certified Coral Frag Registry
one_liner: A genotype registry where reef breeders register mother colonies and buyers verify that a $500 frag is genuinely the named morph.
customer: Coral breeders and vendors, frag-swap organizers, high-end reef hobbyists and aquarium auction sites.
problem: Frags are clones, so one genotype circulates under multiple names and different colonies share a name. Studies of aquarium-trade corals show named morphs and common names are messy, and DNA barcodes do not resolve Acropora from the trade. High-value morphs sell for hundreds to thousands of dollars with no provenance.
solution: Genotype tissue clippings with low-cost SNP or amplicon panels through a partner lab. Breeders register mother genotypes with their signature, buyers mail a clipping (~$40) for a match, vendors display a 'DNA-verified' badge, and a searchable registry prevents duplicate naming and supports lineage and royalty claims.
why_now: Cheap sequencing and ML-based genotype calling make per-sample cost low enough for hobbyists. The research gap between barcodes and genotype identification is now documented.
revenue_model: $40 per verification, $99 breeder registration, a $29/month vendor badge subscription, and royalties on licensed morphs.
non_obvious_insight: In clonal organisms the genotype is the product, yet the market prices names, which are marketing. The first to make genotype searchable creates something like a plant-variety registry, which breeders will fund because it protects their premium. Expect challenges from species-specific panels, symbiont DNA and shipping rules.
first_30_days: Partner with a genomics lab. Test 100 frags from 5 well-known vendors' same-name corals for free and publish any duplicate genotypes sold under multiple names in reefing forums. Sell the first 300 paid tests.

title: Vape Amnesty: Hazmat Pickup Funds Teen Quitting
one_liner: Turn the disposable vape from a fire-prone hazmat problem into the top of a cessation funnel: collect vapes at schools and clinics, send the lithium cells to domestic black-mass buyers, and enroll every person who drops one off in a paid quit program.
customer: School districts and county health departments (using youth-vaping settlement and tobacco-prevention funds), plus health plans, Medicaid programs and state quitlines that pay per enrolled quit attempt. Haulers, MRFs and their insurers are a secondary payer for fire-risk reduction.
problem: Vapes are a named driver of the 2026 battery-fire surge: 74 catastrophic facility fires (over $400K each) year to date versus 71 in all of 2024, and one UK hauler saw about 480,000 vapes in two months. Schools confiscate them by the bucket and either pay for hazmat pickup or bin them (nicotine e-liquid can classify as acute hazardous waste in many states, and the cells are Li-ion). Meanwhile cessation programs cannot find teen and young-adult vapers, who do not self-identify.
solution: A 'drop, quit, ship' kit. Fire-rated locking drop boxes sit in school nurse offices, pharmacies, urgent cares and campus clinics. Each box has a QR code that opens a confidential text-based quit coach, with a telehealth clinician for pharmacotherapy where the user is old enough. A licensed universal-waste hauler batches the vapes, discharges and extracts the cells for black-mass sale, and manifests the e-liquid. Districts get a compliance report and an 'alternative to suspension' curriculum. Public health gets anonymized data on which illicit brands and flavors are turning up.
why_now: The Aug 27, 2026 BIS rule forces black mass to be sold to US buyers, so recovered cells have a guaranteed domestic outlet. Battery-fire counts are at 10-year highs and nobody has decided who pays for the losses. California just expanded battery EPR (SB 501). Youth-vaping settlement money is still being allocated by states and districts.
revenue_model: Per-school or per-clinic annual fee for boxes, pickups and compliance reporting ($1-3K per site). A bounty per enrolled quit attempt from plans and state programs. A small hauler and insurer sponsorship for avoided fire exposure. Black-mass proceeds are trivial (a tonne is roughly 50-100K vapes), so the business runs on the public-health and hazmat budgets, not on the materials.
non_obvious_insight: Two budgets that never talk to each other, public health (which pays for quits but cannot find the user) and waste operations (which finds the user's object but only sees a hazard), both pay to touch the same physical item. A vape in a drop box is a self-identified nicotine-dependent person at peak motivation.
first_30_days: Pitch 3 school districts and 1 county health department on a free 'amnesty week' at two high schools. Buy 10 fire-rated collection containers and sign a licensed universal-waste hauler. White-label an existing text-quit vendor. Collect the first ~200 vapes, count flavors and brands, and publish a one-page fire-risk and quit-enrollment report to convert the pilots into paid annual contracts.

title: Cooler-Door Pivot for THC Beverage Brands
one_liner: A 45-day pivot studio that moves hemp-THC drink and gummy brands into compliant functional products under their existing distributor and retailer slots, plus a per-container THC ledger for distributors and retailers.
customer: Small and mid-size hemp-THC beverage and edible brands, beverage distributors including alcohol-licensed ones, and convenience, liquor and smoke-shop chains holding hemp SKUs. Brands pay for the pivot sprint and co-pack. Distributors and retailers pay a subscription for the SKU ledger.
problem: P.L. 119-37 redefines hemp to 0.4 mg total THC per container. The effective date was pushed from Nov 12 to Dec 11, 2026 by H.R. 6500 (signed Sept 2), while synthetic cannabinoids lose hemp status on Nov 12. The US Hemp Roundtable estimates about 95% of existing products fall outside the new definition, and a typical THC drink has 2-10 mg per can. There is no federal sell-through safe harbor. The industry employs about 350,000 people. Distributors are asking whether alcohol-licensed wholesalers can even accept returns in three-tier states, and operators face a liquidity problem, not a compliance problem.
solution: Two parts. First, an SKU ledger where COAs and pack volumes are converted into per-container total THC (delta-9 plus decarboxylated THCA) and a keep, pull or return status by state, with vendor chargeback letters and a documented disposition trail. Second, a pivot studio that reuses the brand's flavor systems, cans and design to launch adaptogen, functional or non-alcoholic SKUs through a vetted co-packer, so the brand keeps its distributor agreements and planogram slots. An optional bridge licenses the brand to a state-licensed cannabis producer, since licensed dispensaries are unaffected by the federal redefinition.
why_now: The reprieve to Dec 11 gives roughly 10 weeks. Four congressional frameworks are pending: Barr, Van Duyne and Landsman, Comer, and a Sheehy-Klobuchar Senate companion. The ledger works whether Congress bans or regulates, because age-21, testing and labeling regimes would still need lab-verified per-container data. Retailers and distributors are already telling counsel to audit inventory and plan wind-downs, and gummy prices are reported at 30-50% of 2025 levels.
revenue_model: $5-15k fixed fee per brand pivot sprint, plus a 2-5% royalty or co-pack margin on the pivot SKUs. $199-499 per month per distributor or retail chain for the SKU ledger and chargeback tooling. Finder fee on brand-licensing deals to licensed operators.
non_obvious_insight: As Harris Sliwoski puts it, 'The problem for many operators will not be compliance but liquidity' (https://harris-sliwoski.com/cannalawblog/what-the-2026-federal-hemp-ban-means-for-unsold-hemp-inventory/). The scarce asset of a THC-drink brand is not inventory, which is illiquid and repricing downward, but its cooler-door slots and distributor agreements, which are among the hardest things to win in beverages. Those slots vanish if the brand disappears. The per-container standard turns an impossible reformulation into a category switch: LearnBrands notes the demand is being inherited by non-alcoholic beer, alcohol-removed wine and functional beverages (https://www.learnbrands.com/post/hemp-thc-beverage-ban-november-2026). Sources on the reprieve and stakes: https://foleyhoag.com/news-and-insights/blogs/cannabis-and-the-law/2026/september/a-temporary-reprieve-for-hemp-thc-products%E2%80%A6-but-what-now/ and https://www.ediblerank.com/legal/hemp-ban-timeline
first_30_days: Pull 40 THC-beverage brands from distributor and retailer press lists and offer a free exposure scan built from their COAs and volumes. Sell three paid pivot sprints. Line up one co-packer with non-alcoholic and adaptogen capability. Pilot the SKU ledger with two distributors and one c-store chain, producing their pull and return list.

title: Affordable Capital-Stack Solver for Conversion Developers
one_liner: A structuring engine and expert memo that tells first-time affordable developers which subsidy stack is fundable for a given office conversion, with a calendar of deadlines.
customer: Office owners, small and mid developers and nonprofits pursuing conversions on public land or under affordability mandates, and city housing agencies running RFPs.
problem: Conversions are moving to public land and affordable set-asides (NYC's 100 Gold Street grew to 4,000 units with 1,000 affordable). That drags market-rate developers into a 6-8 source stack (4% LIHTC and bonds, land lease, abatements, historic credits, PACE, city and state gap funds) with volume-cap timing and set-aside tradeoffs. Consultants charge $25-75K and take months, and deals die before they start.
solution: Input a building and city, and get the top three feasible stacks with set-aside options, equity pricing ranges, application calendar and funder checklists. A human affordable-housing finance specialist reviews each output and delivers a structuring memo; an add-on kit supports public-land RFP responses.
why_now: The 2025 federal tax law eased the bond test for 4% credits and raised 9% allocations starting 2026. Conversions increasingly require affordability, and distressed-office buyers need a plan quickly.
revenue_model: $8-20K flat structuring memo, a 0.5% success fee on closed subsidy, and $1.5K per month developer subscription.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input is not capital but a first-timer's knowledge of which stack is fundable and when. The winning product is an eligibility-and-calendar engine, not another architect's feasibility study.
first_30_days: Recruit two former affordable-housing finance directors. Publish stack templates for three cities with conversion incentives. Approach 20 office owners and receivers in those cities. Sell three memos at a $6K founder price.

title: Memory Safe-Harbor: Stop Shredding Server DRAM
one_liner: A component-level sanitization policy plus a resale desk that lets neoclouds and enterprises reuse retired DRAM, CPUs and GPUs instead of shredding whole servers.
customer: Neoclouds, colocation operators, banks and healthcare IT asset managers refreshing servers, with ITADs as the channel. They pay a fixed fee and take a resale share.
problem: Data-center hardware turns over in 12-18 months and a GPU server rack can exceed $1M. DRAM is up about 400% since early 2024. Many enterprise policies still shred whole servers, destroying volatile memory that holds no persistent data. One client reportedly gained 'eight figures' just by pre-triaging refurbish versus scrap.
solution: Publish and audit a per-server-model matrix of which components persist data (SSDs, NVDIMMs, BMC and NIC flash, TPMs) and which do not (DIMMs, most compute and mechanical parts). Get it signed off by a security auditor and the client's CISO. Then run the part-out desk. Data-bearing parts are wiped or destroyed with serialized custody. Everything else is graded, tested and sold to secondary buyers.
why_now: The 2025-26 memory price spike turns shredding into a cash-burning act. AI capex has created huge, fast-cycling retiring fleets, and Sumitomo's GreenTek acquisition shows ITAD is being bought as a trading business.
revenue_model: 40-60% resale share to the client after costs, a $10-30K policy and audit fee per client, and a per-serial chain-of-custody fee.
non_obvious_insight: 'Shred everything' is a compliance habit, not a security requirement. The barrier is organizational sign-off, not technology. Whoever ships a pre-approved risk framework gets inventory that no one else can touch.
first_30_days: Write a 10-page component sanitization matrix for the 5 most common GPU and CPU server models. Have a security-audit firm review it. Pitch 10 neocloud and colo IT asset leads and 5 mid-size ITADs. Run a one-rack pilot on revenue share.

title: Closing Ceremonies for Layoffs and Team Sunsets
one_liner: Trained ex-chaplains and celebrants who design and run dignified endings for teams hit by AI-driven layoffs, project sunsets and site closures.
customer: HR and people leaders at mid-size and large firms (500-5,000 employees) restructuring around AI, and outplacement firms that want to bundle a meaning-making service.
problem: Challenger reports AI was cited in about 112,713 announced US job cuts through July 2026 (about 24% of all cuts) and has led all reasons for five straight months. Layoffs are still delivered in a 15-minute video call and followed by résumé workshops. Nobody marks what ended, so leavers feel discarded, survivors feel guilty and disengage, and the company inherits hostile alumni.
solution: A 'Closing' package after legal communications are done: a facilitated last-day ceremony with a witness circle, a symbolic hand-off of work, a leaver-alumni charter (references, introductions), a manager script that bans corporate euphemism, and a survivor circle a week later. It is delivered in person or on video by a trained celebrant or ex-chaplain.
why_now: AI-attributed layoffs have become the leading cause of job cuts in 2026, and waves are recurring. Employer brand and alumni networks now matter for boomerang hiring and recruiting, and workers are openly sceptical of 'AI restructuring' messaging.
revenue_model: $4-12k per event, annual retainers of roughly $30-100k for an 'endings desk' that supports repeated restructurings, per-seat training licences for managers, and channel fees from outplacement partners.
non_obvious_insight: Companies overspend on what people do next and underspend on acknowledging what just ended. A layoff is a funeral without a ritual, and the missing ritual is the root of downstream problems: regretted attrition, employer-brand damage and lost referrals. A ceremony costs a tiny fraction of severance and is the only lever that changes how people talk about the company afterwards.
first_30_days: Recruit three ex-chaplains or celebrants. Build a 2-hour and a half-day format with a legal-review partner. Approach 15 outplacement consultants and 30 people-operations leaders, and offer one discounted team pilot in exchange for a case study.

title: Skill Rooms: Proctored Work-Sample Studios for Hiring
one_liner: Walk-in, device-free testing studios where candidates take a 90-minute employer-designed work sample under ID-verified proctoring, with a portable score that many employers honor.
customer: Staffing firms and mid-size employers hiring entry and mid-level roles (customer support, analysts, junior developers, paralegals, sales development) who are drowning in AI-written applications and AI-assisted interview cheating. Employers pay $75-200 per sitting, candidates pay nothing.
problem: Resumes and cover letters are now noise. In a dataset of about 19,000 live interviews from mid-2025 to early 2026, over a third of candidates showed signs of AI-assisted cheating (close to half in software engineering). Google, Cisco and McKinsey have brought back in-person rounds, but each employer improvising its own on-site test is expensive.
solution: Studios in 10 metros, rented after hours from coworking spaces and community colleges. Fixed-time sittings with ID checks and locked-down machines, and standard job-family work samples (writing under time limit, spreadsheet modeling, code on an air-gapped machine, mock client call), scored by rubric with human review and AI assistance. Candidates get a 'Verified Work Sample' credential valid for 12 months and portable across employers, and employers receive pre-screened slates.
why_now: AI cheating in remote interviews is now measurable and widely reported, in-person verification is returning at large employers, and entry-level applicant floods make cheap, trustworthy screening valuable. Existing proctoring vendors (OnVUE and similar) focus on certification exams, not hiring work samples.
revenue_model: Per-sitting fee from employers, premium pricing for custom work samples, per-hire placement fees through staffing partners, and optional paid practice tests for candidates.
non_obvious_insight: When signals get cheap, standardized proctored tests win, which is how the SAT displaced recommendation letters. The portable score, not the room, is the business: every additional employer that honors it lowers each candidate's cost of proving skill and raises its value, and it gives displaced or credential-less workers a way to prove themselves without a degree.
first_30_days: Rent a 12-seat room in one city and sign 5 staffing agencies hiring for three roles. Design three work samples and rubrics, then run a first cohort of about 40 candidates. Charge employers $125 per candidate who passes, and use the results to sign the next 10 employers on the same score.

title: Harvest-Season Fab Van for Farm Machinery
one_liner: A trailer with industrial printers, a small mill and lathe, and a 3D scanner that parks at grain co-ops during harvest and planting and fabricates the broken part while the farmer waits.
customer: Row-crop and specialty farms, custom harvesters and independent ag-repair shops (Midwest, Plains, Central Valley), plus farm co-ops that host the van.
problem: A combine or planter is worth thousands of dollars a day inside a 10-day weather window. The dealer's part is backordered, discontinued or priced like a ransom. The failed item is usually a $3 plastic or steel piece: a latch, bracket, sensor mount, cab trim, bushing, pin, wear pad or knob.
solution: Two things. First, a mobile print-and-machine unit (carbon-fiber nylon printing, benchtop CNC mill and lathe, handheld scanner) that turns a broken part into a fabricated one in hours. Second, a growing digital parts library indexed by machine make, model and serial number, where every repaired part becomes a reusable file. Farmers can also buy a 'Season Pass' per machine that guarantees fabricated-part turnaround inside 24 hours.
why_now: The FTC and five states settled with Deere on July 8, 2026. For 10 years Deere must give farmers and independent shops the same repair software and resources it gives dealers, and it separately agreed to a $99M class settlement. That will grow independent repair shops, and parts are the next bottleneck. Crop margins are tight, so cheaper aftermarket parts sell, and harvest is happening right now.
revenue_model: Per-part fabrication ($40 to $600, with a rush premium), Season Pass subscriptions ($1k to $2.5k per machine per season), wholesale to independent repair shops, and a co-op hosting fee or revenue share.
non_obvious_insight: Farmers don't buy parts. They buy hours inside a weather window, so price against downtime avoided, not material cost. The scanned-part library by machine serial number is the compounding moat. Every emergency job builds the catalog that later lets you ship parts remotely, and the van is really a data-acquisition vehicle.
first_30_days: Borrow or rent a machine shop and start with two industrial printers, a benchtop mill and a scanner (about $40k to $60k), or begin with a used trailer. Sign two independent ag-repair shops and one co-op as hosts. Run a 'we fix it while you wait' pilot through the rest of this harvest, charging from job one. Post before/after photos in local farm Facebook groups and to elevator and co-op newsletters. Log every part as a file.

title: Recovery Units: Hospital Step-Down in Lease-Up Apartments
one_liner: Master-lease vacant units in lease-up apartment buildings near hospitals and rent them by the night as staffed 7-30 day recovery apartments for patients who have no safe home to be discharged to.
customer: Hospital care-management and ACO budgets, plus Medicare Advantage and Medicaid plans, pay per diem. Apartment owners get guaranteed rent.
problem: Hospitals hold medically ready patients because home is unsafe, absent or far away. Those avoidable days are commonly cited at $2,500+ each, skilled-nursing beds are scarce, and hospital-at-home programs exclude patients without a suitable home. In the same metros 1.2M apartment units sit in lease-up, with concessions on about 16% of stabilized units (21% in the South, 37% in Austin). Owners of stalled lease-ups need occupancy and real rent, not another free month.
solution: A 10-20 unit block per hospital cluster: furnished, accessible, with home-health nursing and PT visits, meal delivery, a caregiver check-in line and a nurse-led transition plan. Bill a bundled per diem of roughly $175-300 against the $2,500+ hospital day. Owners get a 12-24 month master lease at near face rent with no concession.
why_now: The 2026 lease-up glut and 34-day lease times make owners receptive to any non-haggling tenant. Enhanced ACA subsidies expired and Medicaid work requirements arrive in Jan 2027, so hospitals face rising uncompensated care and margin pressure and are hunting for cheaper post-acute options.
revenue_model: Per-diem revenue minus master-lease and service costs (illustratively $50-80/day margin at 70% occupancy); later capitated arrangements with plans.
non_obvious_insight: A lease-up owner values a tenant that pays full rent on a unit that would otherwise carry a concession, and a hospital values the cheapest safe bed it has ever been offered. The two budgets have never touched because no one operates in between.
first_30_days: Find one lease-up property within 5 miles of a hospital that is running 20%+ concessions. Negotiate 5 units on a 6-month master lease with a 60-day out. Sign a home-health agency. Pitch the hospital's case-management director to trial 10 discharges and invoice per diem in month 2. Check local short-stay rules first and use a 30-day minimum license with early-release credits where needed.

title: Collections That Hunt the Payer, Not the Patient
one_liner: A contingency-fee receivables firm for ambulance agencies and ER physician groups that, within 30 days of a self-pay bill, screens the patient for retroactive Medicaid eligibility and files the application for them, turning accounts debt buyers would take at 2-4 cents into full Medicaid payments.
customer: County and municipal EMS agencies, their outsourced ambulance-billing companies, and independent ER, anesthesia and radiology physician groups in Medicaid-expansion states. Rural hospitals under 100 beds are the second wave.
problem: Self-pay accounts sit through 90-180 days of statements before they go to an agency or get sold to a debt buyer, and buyers pay only pennies (a few cents on the dollar for medical accounts). Most states let Medicaid reach back only about 3 months before the application date, so by the time a normal collections workflow gives up, the window in which a real payer could have been found has already closed. Patients get dunned for money they may never have owed, and the provider recovers almost nothing.
solution: Take a nightly feed of new self-pay accounts (demographics only, under a BAA). Screen each one for likely Medicaid or charity-care eligibility. Contact the patient in the first two weeks with a simple offer: we complete your Medicaid application for free. Then file the application, chase documents and caseworkers, and bill Medicaid retroactively for the provider. Patients who do not qualify are routed to charity care or a payment plan, and nobody is ever dunned. The firm is paid a contingency on Medicaid dollars actually collected. The dashboard shows each account's days left in the retro window, so providers see the clock that traditional collections ignore.
why_now: The 2025 budget law (OBBBA) cuts Medicaid retroactive coverage to 1 month for expansion adults and 2 months for everyone else, for applications from January 2027. From then on every day of delay burns covered dates, so speed to application becomes the whole product. Providers are also under revenue pressure, states keep passing medical-debt limits that make selling accounts harder, and Medicaid redetermination and work-requirement churn in 2027 makes eligibility-navigation skills scarce and valuable.
revenue_model: 15-20% contingency on Medicaid reimbursements recovered, with an optional $1-2k/month platform fee for charity-care and medical-debt compliance reporting. Ambulance and physician-group accounts are small ($800-$2,500 each) but high in volume and nearly free to service once the screening flow is built.
non_obvious_insight: Collections looks like a persuasion business but is really a timing business. Every step of the traditional workflow (statements, calls, placement at day 120 or later) pushes action past the point where a third-party payer can still be found. Run the workflow backwards, find the payer inside 30 days, and you get the rare collections company that patients thank you for and that pays the provider 10-30x what a debt buyer would.
first_30_days: Pick one expansion state with a 3-month retro window. Hire two ex-hospital eligibility reps and one engineer. Offer 3 county EMS agencies or their billing companies a free back-test of the last 12 months of self-pay accounts, showing how many were eligible and inside a window where enrollment would have paid. Convert the best result into a contingency pilot on new accounts, ideally with an existing certified navigator status. First Medicaid approvals typically land 45-90 days after filing, so signed pilots come in month 1 and cash in months 3-4.

title: Court-Safe Esper Machine From Bystander Video
one_liner: Blade Runner's Esper machine, made honest: a scaled, non-generative 3D reconstruction of an accident scene from mixed dashcam, doorbell, CCTV and phone clips, with error bars built to survive an admissibility challenge.
customer: Personal-injury law firms, insurer subrogation and special-investigation units, defense counsel and municipal risk managers, initially in disputed-liability vehicle and pedestrian cases with three or more video clips.
problem: Cases turn on several shaky clips. Traditional reconstruction by an expert costs thousands of dollars and takes weeks. Generative 'enhancement' gets challenged or excluded because AI invents pixels, and Gaussian-splat models look convincing but have no verified real-world scale.
solution: Ingest all clips, time-sync them (audio fingerprints, sirens, shared events), solve camera poses, and recover metric scale automatically from regulated-size objects in frame: lane-stripe cycles, stop and speed signs, crosswalk widths, license plates and standard curb heights. Output a measurable model with per-measurement error bars and a 'no generated pixels' guarantee (every pixel traceable to a source frame), plus vehicle speed and trajectory estimates and sightline views ('could the driver see the pedestrian?'). A partner licensed reconstructionist signs the report and serves as expert of record.
why_now: Feed-forward multi-view reconstruction and Gaussian splatting made casual-video reconstruction cheap in the last two years. Courts and defense bars are actively litigating AI-enhanced video. Doorbell, dashcam and storefront cameras mean most incidents now have several angles.
revenue_model: $900-2,500 per case, a discount tier for firms on subscription, and an expert-testimony fee split with the reconstructionist.
non_obvious_insight: Admissibility, not photorealism, is the product. Lawyers would rather have an ugly model with error bars than a beautiful hallucination, and automatic metric scale from objects whose dimensions are set by traffic-control standards is the unlock that separates this from generic splat tools and from drone-only videogrammetry.
first_30_days: Recruit one reconstructionist as expert of record. Offer 10 PI firms a free second-opinion reconstruction on live cases with at least three clips, then charge $1,200 for the next. Target five paying cases by day 90 and a written methods statement reviewed by a litigator.

title: Emeritus: Paying 80-Year-Old Tradespeople for Tacit Knowledge
one_liner: Recruit retired machinists, lineworkers, boiler operators and railroad and telephone technicians in their 70s-90s, pay them hourly to teach on camera, and sell the corpus to AI labs, robotics companies and industrial firms.
customer: Robotics and embodied-AI labs, LLM data buyers who have exhausted white-collar experts, and utilities and plants that run 1970s-era equipment.
problem: The last generation with hand skills and legacy-system judgment is disappearing. Companies try to capture knowledge from employees before retirement with KM software, but the deepest experts left years ago and can't be reached by enterprise tools. AI labs pay $75-200+/hr to lawyers and doctors through Mercor and Surge but have thin coverage of physical-process knowledge. Retirees are invisible to gig platforms.
solution: A field-producer model. Partner with union retiree clubs, trade associations and retiree chapters (IBEW, IAM, railroad retiree groups). Send a two-person crew with a phone rig and lav mics to sit with each retiree in their garage, shop or a plant visit. Run structured 'teach-back' sessions on failure modes, sounds, smells and shortcuts. Transcribe, segment and tag with AI. Pay the expert $60-120/hr plus a royalty share when the corpus is licensed. Sell curated, rights-cleared datasets and 'ask the old-timer' search seats to plants.
why_now: AI labs are spending heavily on expert data (Mercor reportedly pays contractors about $1.5M a day), and humanoid and robotics teams need process knowledge. About 40% of the manufacturing workforce is retirement-eligible within a decade, and utilities report up to half pension-eligible by 2027. Multimodal models can now ingest video and audio at scale.
revenue_model: Dataset licensing per hour of tagged, rights-cleared sessions ($500-2,000/hr). Enterprise capture projects ($30-150k). Per-seat search and Q&A licenses. Expert royalties are a cost of goods, which is also the recruiting pitch.
non_obvious_insight: The scarcest expert data isn't PhDs but the 82-year-old who can diagnose a turbine by sound. Retirees are also the only experts with no employer NDA or IP claim, so their data rights are cleaner and they can sign licenses directly. For the elder, it is paid, respected work and social contact, which is what tech never offers 80-year-olds.
first_30_days: Pick one niche (say retired tool-and-die makers or utility lineworkers) and recruit through three retiree-association newsletters. Pay 15 experts $100/hr for 2-hour sessions and produce about 30 hours. Have a lawyer draft consent and licensing contracts with cognitive-capacity safeguards and a family representative. Send samples to 3 robotics companies and 2 utilities.

title: Landlord Loan Radar for Office Tenants
one_liner: Monitoring and lease-audit software that warns small office tenants when their landlord's loan is heading for trouble and recovers overbilled operating expenses.
customer: Tenants of 3,000-40,000 sf in office buildings (law, accounting, medical, nonprofit), their tenant-rep brokers, and office managers.
problem: With 17.8% national vacancy, 13.2% office CMBS delinquency and $39B maturing in a year, tenants sign renewals blind to the landlord's debt cliff. Distressed landlords may stop funding improvements or cut services, and operating-expense pass-throughs (gross-up, admin-fee caps, capital items) are often mis-billed, especially at low occupancy. Only large tenants can afford audit consultants.
solution: Public CMBS loan-level filings feed a radar that alerts on maturity dates, DSCR or occupancy drops and special-servicing transfers. An opex audit takes a lease and annual reconciliation and flags gross-up and base-year errors and non-recoverable capital costs. A 'renewal leverage brief' shows when the landlord needs an extension to refinance.
why_now: Elevated vacancy gives tenants leverage, distress is at a multi-year high, and document-reading software makes small-lease audits economical.
revenue_model: $149-299 per month per lease for monitoring, 25-30% success fee on recovered overbilling, and a white-label version for tenant-rep brokers.
non_obvious_insight: The landlord's refinancing deadline is public but nobody reads it, and a lease extension is exactly what a lender wants to see. A tenant who knows this can trade a signature for concessions.
first_30_days: Build a watchlist for three metros from public CMBS filings. Offer a free 'is your building on the list' checker and email 500 small firms in those buildings. Sell success-fee audits to the first five responders.

title: Buffet Lab: Hotel Breakfast Lines as Test Market
one_liner: Paid two-week trials that put reformulated or novel ingredients on real hotel and cruise breakfast lines, with item-level consumption, waste and hot-hold colour data.
customer: Food manufacturers facing the FDA petroleum-dye phase-out, and makers of natural colours and alternative proteins such as fermentation whey, rubisco and purple-sweet-potato colour, including farmer-owned processors. Hotels and cruise operators are the supply side.
problem: Dye reformulation costs $50K-$500K per SKU and takes 12-24+ months, and Walmart private label goes dye-free in January 2027. Whey is short and alt-protein funding has collapsed, so startups need cheap real-world proof. Lab sensory panels and retail test markets are slow, expensive and blind to failure modes like colour fade under lights, texture after hot-hold, and portion rejection by the roughly 12% of Americans on GLP-1s.
solution: Recruit 30-50 independent hotels plus one cruise or resort operator. Supply product free and track item-level consumption against control, plate waste, restock rates by daypart, QR feedback, hot-hold time and light exposure, with colorimeter photos of colour drift. Optionally A/B half-portions. Deliver a two-week acceptance, waste and stability report, and sell recurring access to the panel to CPG innovation teams.
why_now: The FDA dye phase-out targets December 2027, with 22 states adding food-restriction rules and a federal ultra-processed food definition in review. Whey concentrate is up 108% in two years, alt-protein funding fell to $881M in 2025 with only $197M in H1 2026, and GLP-1 users are reshaping portions and protein preferences. Buyers want supply-risk answers, not sustainability stories.
revenue_model: $12K-$30K per product trial. Hotels receive product, about $40/day and waste analytics. Panel subscriptions for CPG innovation teams of $60K-$120K/yr.
non_obvious_insight: A hotel breakfast line is the largest measurable eating experiment in commerce: repeat business travellers, captive choice, fixed hot-hold time and lighting, and a natural weigh-back at clearing. It stress-tests exactly the things that kill natural-colour and protein reformulations, much faster than a retail test market.
first_30_days: Recruit 8 independent hotels via an owners' association and approach 5 natural-colour and ingredient startups directly. Run one paid pilot, for example a dye-free pastry glaze or cereal, at about $8K to prove the report format.

title: Remote Second-RN for Rural Night Shifts
one_liner: A pool of remote nurses that acts as the recorded, independent second person on video for narcotic waste, blood checks and high-alert drug double-checks when a rural hospital has three nurses on at 3am.
customer: Chief nursing officers and pharmacy directors at critical access hospitals (25 beds or fewer, roughly 1,300 in the US), plus the malpractice and captive insurers that cover them. Hospitals pay a monthly subscription.
problem: Policy requires a second licensed person to witness controlled-substance waste and to independently double-check insulin, heparin, blood and pediatric doses. At night at a rural hospital that second person is a nurse who is mid-code or mid-admission. Every nurse knows the witness signature is often given without actually watching. That is the most common way nurses divert drugs, and it is also how honest nurses end up with paper trails that would not survive an audit. The hospital cannot prove the witness happened. The other option is waking a colleague from another unit, which delays care.
solution: Start with a $150 tablet-and-camera cart at the dispensing cabinet. A remote RN appears on video within 60 seconds, watches the waste happen, and attests in a portal. The system keeps a time-stamped video clip and an audit log matched to the cabinet's waste records, exported as a PDF for the diversion committee. Then add two-RN blood transfusion verification, independent double-checks for high-alert drugs, and a 'second set of eyes' call for pediatric dosing. Do no EHR integration at first. Matching by timestamp is enough to sell.
why_now: The Bluesight 2026 State of Hospital Pharmacy report says about 63% of health-system leaders reported at least one diversion incident in the past year, and waste is a top diversion method because witnessing is loosely policed. Virtual nursing has become normal since 2024, and the Nurse Licensure Compact now covers most states, so one remote nurse can cover many hospitals. State Rural Health Transformation Program money is flowing, with every state having posted at least one funding opportunity by August 2026, and workforce and quality dollars can pay for this. Whether remote-video witnessing is acceptable is mostly a hospital-policy and pharmacy and therapeutics committee decision, but each state's board of pharmacy and nursing board should be checked before launch.
revenue_model: $1,500-2,500 per hospital per month, plus a per-event fee for transfusion and double-check calls above a set volume. A typical rural ED has 10-25 waste events a night at 2-3 minutes each, so one remote RN can cover roughly 8-12 hospitals per night. Estimated gross margin is 40-50%. A secondary revenue line is a discount arrangement with medical liability insurers, who benefit from the audit trail.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone selling diversion software (analytics, cabinet data mining, waste-testing) tries to detect diversion after the fact. Insiders know the root problem is that no real second person exists at night in a small hospital. You do not need better detection. You need to supply the missing colleague, cheaply and on camera. The service also protects honest nurses, who will therefore support it and not resist it.
first_30_days: Recruit 6 per-diem or retired RNs with compact licenses who want remote night hours at $35-40/hr. Use an off-the-shelf tablet with a recording app and a simple web portal that produces the PDF log. Offer free 30-day pilots to two critical access hospitals through the founder nurse's own pharmacy director and CNO. Get the pilot approved as a policy amendment at the pharmacy and therapeutics committee. Convert to a $1,500 monthly contract after 30 days if the audit log is shown to the diversion committee and the hospital's insurer.

title: Remote-Piloted Care Robots: Labor by Teleoperation
one_liner: Mobile manipulators supervised by remote pilots handle non-clinical night-shift chores in memory care, importing labor by bandwidth instead of visa.
customer: Memory-care and assisted-living operators (night and evening shifts), later affluent solo agers at home. The buyer is the operations executive with a labor budget.
problem: Night ratios of about 1:20 mean chores (water rounds, linen, trash, fetching supplies) compete with clinical rounds. Every open aide slot costs $45-60k with overtime. The 2026 visa pause closes the foreign-labor route.
solution: Off-the-shelf mobile manipulators (a Hello Robot Stretch-class robot, about $25k, and later humanoids) supervised by a bilingual remote pilot network trained on non-clinical tasks, with one pilot overseeing 3-4 robots. The first product is a night-shift runner: water and linen rounds, trash, fetch, room tidy, and a face-and-voice response to call lights that routes to a human aide. No lifting of residents and no clinical tasks.
why_now: Consumer humanoids with human-teleop fallback (1X's NEO opened preorders in late 2025), cheap mobile manipulators and vision-language-action models make assisted autonomy feasible in 2026. Wisconsin nursing homes' failed overseas-labor plan shows demand for labor by any route.
revenue_model: Robot-as-a-service at about $4,500 a month per robot for 12 hours a day (roughly $12-15 an hour against a $28-35 loaded aide cost), plus implementation fees.
non_obvious_insight: The moat is the pilot network, the safety case and the ops playbook, not the hardware. Teleoperation turns overseas labor into a service delivered without a visa, and a human-in-the-loop model works long before full autonomy.
first_30_days: Lease two Stretch-class robots and recruit six pilots from a Manila BPO. Run a free two-week night-shift pilot in one memory-care community, log chores and aide-minutes saved, and collect LOIs.

title: Spray-Drone Service Depots for Grounded Fleets
one_liner: Independent repair, parts and loaner service for the roughly 80% of US spray drones that are DJI Agras.
customer: Custom aerial applicators, ag retailers and farm co-ops running spray-drone fleets.
problem: DJI was added to the FCC Covered List in December 2025, new T55 and T100 models have no committed US launch, and applicators face limited drones and parts.
solution: A depot network with a parts pool, battery service, pump and arm repair, calibration and a loaner fleet, plus operator training and compliance support.
why_now: The ban freezes new models while the installed base must keep flying for years, and everyone else is chasing US-made OEM hardware.
revenue_model: Repair fees, parts margin and annual maintenance contracts per drone.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody builds a service moat because the attention goes to replacement hardware. The installed base is the durable revenue pool and needs only lawful repair and parts.
first_30_days: Buy a starter parts inventory, set up a depot in one spray-heavy region such as the Texas or Arkansas Delta, and sign 10 applicators to maintenance contracts.

title: Pull-the-Plug Testing for Hospitals and Water Plants
one_liner: Bring data center-grade full-facility blackout testing to hospitals, water utilities and other critical facilities that never actually pull the plug, and help them source scarce backup gear the AI build-out has hoarded.
customer: Critical-access and rural hospitals, water and wastewater districts, 911 centers, cold-chain warehouses and municipal facilities. Secondary payers: property insurers, hospital captives and risk pools that can subsidize tests or discount premiums for certified resilience.
problem: Routine emergency-power testing is usually a short, partial-load generator run. It rarely exercises the whole chain (utility loss, ATS transfer, sequenced load pickup, cooling, fuel supply, paralleling controls) under real load, so the interaction failures show up during the actual storm or grid event. At the same time the AI build-out has swallowed generator, switchgear and transformer production, with multi-year lead times, so a failed generator or breaker at a small hospital cannot be replaced quickly. Facility managers know their fragile points but have no credible way to test them or to find spares.
solution: A one-day 'controlled blackout' service using data center IST discipline: written sequence-of-operations script, load-bank top-up to real facility load, thermographic and breaker health checks before and after, a witnessed utility-loss transfer, fuel/cooling/ventilation checks, and a punch list. Deliver a resilience certificate with prioritized fixes and remaining-life estimates. Upsell: source and retest certified pre-owned generators, ATS and switchgear from cancelled or paused data center orders, and keep a small regional spares pool for members of a hospital or water-district cooperative.
why_now: AI infrastructure is consuming electrical gear supply (transformer lead times of 3-5 years, switchgear reportedly sold out into 2028) while nearly half of planned 2026 US data center builds are delayed or canceled, which leaves stranded but scarce gear. Storm and grid-stress events are also raising the stakes for small critical facilities. Insurers are scrutinizing resilience, and rural facilities cannot afford the big-firm engineering studies.
revenue_model: $18K-45K per facility test; annual re-test contracts; 10-15% sourcing margin on certified pre-owned gear; insurer or captive partnership fees per policyholder tested; small monthly membership for spares-pool access.
non_obvious_insight: In a data center nobody trusts backup power until someone has pulled the plug at full load, and most first tests find something. The rest of critical infrastructure, which arguably matters more, almost never does this because the fear of a failed test outweighs the fear of a failed emergency. A Cx lead who has run hundreds of pull-the-plug tests can make the test routine and safe. The AI boom also turns the spare-gear problem into a secondary market that only someone who has seen the cancellations firsthand can source from.
first_30_days: Rent a 500 kW-1 MW load bank and partner with an electrical contractor. Call 10 facility directors at critical-access hospitals and rural water districts through state hospital and rural water associations. Offer 2 discounted first tests in exchange for case studies and insurer introductions. Approach one regional property insurer or hospital captive with a loss-prevention pilot. Start a private list of sellers of surplus gensets and switchgear from paused data center projects.

title: Worker-Owned Agentic Back-Office Cooperatives
one_liner: A franchise-in-a-box that helps laid-off finance and admin staff form co-ops running agent-leveraged bookkeeping, payroll and billing services for local small businesses, keeping the surplus themselves.
customer: Small businesses (5-50 employees) pay $600-2,500 a month. The co-ops pay a 5-8% platform fee, and are financed by cooperative-lending CDFIs, SBA microloans and workforce boards.
problem: The AI productivity dividend flows to platform owners while back-office workers lose jobs. Small businesses lack trusted human accountability (Bench's Dec 2024 shutdown stranded about 35k SMBs), and pure-AI bookkeepers still need a human on the hook.
solution: Co-op charter templates under state worker-co-op law, a shared agent stack (ledger automation, document intake, reconciliation) so each member handles 30-60 clients, a shared E&O policy, bank account and brand, client acquisition through local CPAs and chambers, and patronage dividends. Six-week onboarding.
why_now: Agentic accounting can now handle high-volume categorisation and reconciliation, finance-ops layoffs are rising, Bench's collapse left an opening, and co-op-friendly state laws and CDFI capital exist.
revenue_model: 5-8% of co-op revenue as a platform fee, tooling margin and $5-10k implementation fees per co-op.
non_obvious_insight: Ownership is the lever: workers who own the margin adopt agents fully, whereas employees hide productivity gains for fear of layoff. The scarce asset is trusted local human accountability, and agents supply the cost side.
first_30_days: Find 8-10 laid-off bookkeepers and controllers in one metro through layoff communities. Form a pilot co-op with a co-op legal clinic. Sign 15 SMB clients via three local CPAs and a chamber and run the first monthly closes.
